normalized.governing_thought: Keep buying housings in 2027 and spend on supply resilience, not machinery — the owned cell breaks the board's limits and the lease's edge is too thin to bet on
executive_summary: The owned cell is not a 2027 option. It needs $7.3M against the $5.0M capital limit and would leave ~$3.2M of year-end cash, below the $4.0M floor. The circulated “$27 saving” is $16 per good housing in 2027 once freight, scrap and fixed cost are counted; payback is 3.7 years at 100k units (7.2 at 65k), not “under three”.

Leasing is a cost near-tie that turns negative if any one assumption slips. Over 2027–29 the lease saves $0.3M (1%) versus buying in the planning case, but costs $1.4M more in the conservative demand case and $0.5M more if it runs only seven months of 2027. It needs ≥207k units in 2028–29 just to break even.

Delivery reliability is a supply-design problem that buying can fix faster than any cell. The 0.2-point shortfall (96.8% vs 97% on time) traces to one flood closure. Buffer stock, a tooled alternate shop, 40k reserved units and an emergency supplier act in 0–13 weeks — a cell needs 5–9+ months — for $0.25M of capital and up to $0.72M of working capital.

Pre-agreed gates would switch the answer to the lease; act before the March 2027 quote expiry. Trigger the lease if 2028–29 volume is firmly committed at ≥208k units, the supplier's 2028–29 delivered price exceeds ~$84 (or ~$74 with committed volume), or on-time delivery stays below 97% for two quarters. The plan keeps 2027 year-end cash near $8.2M.

slides.title: The decision has to pass four tests — affordability, like-for-like cost, delivery reliability and robustness — not a unit-price comparison

claims.claim: Terms as quoted for the three options
evidence: Unit cost per good unit: Buy $73 gate + $2 freight/QA = $75; Lease $49 per start → $52.13 yr 1, $51.04 later; Own $46 per start → $50.00 yr 1, $47.92 later
Upfront cash: Buy none, optional $0.25M alternate-shop tooling; Lease $2.0M installation and training; Own $7.3M ($6.5M equipment + $0.8M install)
Fixed cost per year: Buy none; Lease $1.60M lease and staffing; Own $0.75M staffing
Scrap, year 1 / later: Buy covered by price (pays good units only); Lease 6% / 4% of starts; Own 8% / 4% of starts
Practical capacity: Buy up to 140k if renewed; Lease 125k accepted units; Own 120k accepted units
Time to first output: Buy in place, quote valid to March 2027; Lease ~5 months, if site survey passes; Own 9-month equipment lead time + install
After 2029: Buy 2028–29 price and capacity indicative; Lease terminable, no residual value; Own resale ~$2.1M (non-binding)

claims.claim: Four tests the answer must pass
evidence: 1 Affordability: ≤ $5.0M new 2027 capital and year-end cash > $4.0M (from $9.2M today, no new debt or equity)
2 Like-for-like cost: Lowest total cost per good unit over 2027–29, in both planning (300k) and conservative (230k) demand
3 Delivery reliability: ≥ 97% of units shipped within ten business days, plus an executable outage contingency
4 Robustness: Answer holds if demand, scrap, supplier price or start-up timing move against it

claims.claim: The customer mandates delivery reliability and dimensional quality — not insourcing.
Housing volumes are not guaranteed
evidence: the conservative case cuts 2028 from 100k to 65k units

slides.title: Our starting hypothesis — lease a flexible cell — failed three of the five conditions it needed, so we changed the answer to “buy and de-risk”

claims.claim: 4 Buying cannot be made reliable enough to meet 97% — Not supported

slides.title: Where the briefing pack left a choice open we made and logged it; most choices tilt toward the cells, so they do not flatter the case for buying

claims.claim: Choices made and their rationale/effect
evidence: Horizon 2027–29: Matches the pack's volume data, lease termination point and resale date; later years not modelled

Alternate-shop unit price = supplier quote †: Pack gives only the $0.25M tooling charge; to be confirmed by quote
Buffer = 6 weeks at 1,600 units/week: Bridges the emergency supplier's six-week notice; assumes 50 shipping weeks; carrying cost excluded †
Demo yield of 98.5% not used: Excludes start-up runs, rework and downtime; engineer's 8% first-year scrap used instead
Machine-shop correlation not used: Confounded by volume and product mix; no before/after evidence of a causal effect

alternatives_considered.treatment: Included as layer 4 of the contingency (framework agreement, 6 weeks' notice, ~$15/unit premium ≈ $0.1M per month of full outage); described as cheaper protection than the lease unless an outage longer than a year is expected.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: All figures nominal, pre-tax and undiscounted unless stated; based solely on the internal briefing pack; briefing data is synthetic.
Housing volumes are not guaranteed: the conservative case cuts 2028 from 100k to 65k units.
Supplier price after March 2027 is only indicative: each +$1 on 2028–29 adds $0.22M to buying; above ~$84 the lease wins outright.
Contingency not in place in time: a 2027 outage before the buffer and second source exist could breach 97%.
Demand above plan (> 140k after 2029): supplier capacity binds; strengthens the case for a cell from 2029.
Demand below plan strengthens buying: lease −$1.4M, owned cell −$3.5M in the conservative case.
Alternate-shop price and quality unknown: splitting orders may cost more than $75 per good unit; alternate-shop unit price assumed equal to supplier quote.
Inventory carrying cost not modelled: at an assumed 25% a year the buffer adds ~$0.5M over 2027–29; conservative-case ranking unchanged.
Indirect loss of the customer designation unquantified: a large value could justify paying for in-house control.
Nominal, pre-tax, undiscounted basis: discounting penalises upfront-heavy options most, so it would strengthen buying.
Horizon 2027–29; later years not modelled.
Full-year 2027 operation assumed for both cells — physically impossible (5- and 9-month lead times), but favours the cells; partial-year tested on p. 9.
Supplier cost = $73 + $2 = $75 per good unit; the $75 procurement figure is the same quote, not a second one.
Emergency supplier = $88 + $2 freight/QA; pack does not say whether $88 is delivered.
Year-end cash = $9.2M − incremental 2027 outflow; assumes the rest of the business is cash-neutral; buy is charged its $0.72M buffer, cells are not.
Lease $2.0M counted against the $5.0M capital limit.
Buffer = 6 weeks at 1,600 units/week; assumes 50 shipping weeks; carrying cost excluded.
Demo yield of 98.5% not used; engineer's 8% first-year scrap used instead.
Machine-shop correlation not used: confounded by volume and product mix; no before/after evidence of a causal effect.
Resale ~$2.1M for the owned cell is a non-binding dealer indication.
Lease timing assumes the site survey passes; cell timings exclude ramp-up.
Meridian has never run a production cell; the quoted 6% first-year lease scrap is unproven.
Items marked † (emergency supplier freight, alternate-shop unit price, buffer carrying cost) would most benefit from management confirmation before the January decision.
Owners are proposed roles, to be confirmed by the Executive Committee.
